title: Scientists Use Light to Master Magnetism and Topology in Atomically Thin Materials
body:
A team of physicists has demonstrated that a single layer of a two‑dimensional crystal can have its magnetic order and electronic topology switched on and off with pulses of light, opening a route to ultra‑low‑power computing elements that operate without the heat‑generating currents of conventional transistors. The breakthrough, achieved by exposing an atomically thin ferromagnet to carefully tuned laser bursts, shows that photons can act as a reversible “knob” for both spin alignment and the topological character of electronic bands, a combination that has so far remained elusive in solid‑state platforms.

The researchers focused on a van‑der‑Waals material known as chromium triiodide (CrI₃), a magnetic insulator that retains ferromagnetic order down to the monolayer limit. By placing the monolayer on a substrate of hexagonal boron nitride and sandwiching it between graphene electrodes, they created a device that allowed simultaneous optical access and electrical readout. When a femtosecond laser pulse of specific wavelength and intensity struck the crystal, the magnetic moments of the chromium atoms reoriented, effectively toggling the material between a ferromagnetic and a paramagnetic state. Crucially, the same optical stimulus also altered the band structure so that the material switched between a trivial insulator and a topological insulator, a phase distinguished by conducting edge states that are protected against scattering.

The ability to control magnetism with light is not new in itself, but the simultaneous manipulation of topology marks a significant advance. In conventional spintronic devices, magnetic bits are flipped by passing electric currents through nanowires, a process that inevitably dissipates energy as heat. Optical control sidesteps this limitation because photons carry angular momentum without charge, allowing spin reorientation without Joule heating. Moreover, the topological switch adds a new dimension: edge channels that can transport charge or spin with near‑zero resistance could be turned on only when needed, dramatically reducing standby power consumption.

The findings build on a growing body of work exploring “light‑matter” interactions in low‑dimensional systems. Earlier studies showed that circularly polarized light can induce transient magnetization in nonmagnetic semiconductors, while recent experiments demonstrated Floquet engineering—using periodic driving fields to reshape electronic bands—in graphene and transition‑metal dichalcogenides. What sets this work apart is the demonstration of a stable, reversible phase transition at room temperature compatible with device architectures. The team employed time‑resolved Kerr rotation and transport measurements to confirm that the light‑induced states persist for microseconds, long enough for practical switching cycles, and that the process can be repeated thousands of times without degradation.

Industry analysts see immediate implications for next‑generation memory and logic technologies. Magnetic random‑access memory (MRAM) already promises non‑volatile storage with faster write speeds than flash, but its reliance on spin‑transfer torque still incurs energy penalties. An optically driven counterpart could achieve sub‑nanosecond switching with negligible thermal budget, a key requirement for data centers aiming to curb power usage. In addition, the topological edge modes could be harnessed for fault‑tolerant quantum computing, where protected states are less susceptible to decoherence. Integrating such materials with existing silicon photonics platforms may enable hybrid chips that process information both electronically and optically on the same wafer.

Looking ahead, the challenge will be to scale the phenomenon from laboratory flakes to wafer‑scale production and to identify other two‑dimensional compounds that exhibit similar dual control. The researchers are already exploring layered magnets such as Fe₃GeTe₂ and MnBi₂Te₄, which may offer stronger coupling between light and spin or operate at even lower photon energies. If successful, the ability to toggle magnetic order and topological protection with a flash of light could redefine how future computers manage energy, ushering in an era of photonic‑spintronic devices that compute at the speed of light while staying cool.
